Intact

in-TAKT — sounds like 'in tact'; think 'in one piece': untouched and whole. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Intact is whole and undamaged; complete with nothing missing.

Amazingly, the ancient vase was found intact after the earthquake.

Worked Example

A tornado levels half the neighborhood overnight. But one house on the corner still stands with every window whole and every shingle in place. Even the flowerpots on the porch never tipped over.

The house came through completely undamaged — it is intact. Unlike 'repaired,' which means fixed after damage, intact means never damaged in the first place.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

undamaged: Undamaged means not harmed in any way, and it looks at each piece by itself. Intact adds completeness: the whole thing, undamaged and with nothing missing. Two undamaged volumes of a three-volume set are in fine shape, but the set itself is not intact.

whole: Whole means complete, with no parts missing — every piece accounted for. Intact means the thing is whole and also undamaged: nothing chipped, cracked, or torn. A jigsaw puzzle can be whole with every piece in the box and still not intact if half the pieces are bent.

unbroken: Unbroken means not broken or interrupted, and it rules out just one kind of harm — nothing has snapped or shattered. Intact rules out every kind of damage and adds that nothing is missing. A dropped mug can be unbroken yet badly scratched; an intact one shows no harm at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

shattered: broken into many pieces

damaged: harmed or partly broken

Where it sits · how close to perfect condition — usable → intact → pristine

usable vs. intact: Usable is weaker than intact — a usable phone still works despite its scratches, while an intact one has no damage at all.

pristine vs. intact: Pristine is stronger than intact: an intact book is undamaged, but a pristine one looks as perfect as the day it was printed.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — tact-

root — tact-: touched (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin in- (not) plus tactus (touched) means 'not touched.' Something intact has never been touched by harm — still whole and complete.

Use the root in a new word: contact

Use the root in a new word: contact: The astronauts made contact with mission control after the landing.

Root Check

Word Choice

Intact usually follows a verb rather than preceding a noun — things 'remain intact,' 'survive intact,' or 'arrive intact.'
